blocks.text: A loop repeats a block of code so you do not have to write it again and again. Want to print the numbers 1 to 100? A loop does it in three lines instead of a hundred.

blocks.alt: Loop types: for, while, do-while, nested loops

blocks.text: Loops are one of the biggest jumps in what you can build. Almost every real program repeats some work, whether it is going through a list, retrying a task, or running until the user quits.
Loops are how computers do repetitive work tirelessly and instantly. Once you master them, whole categories of problems open up.
Imagine printing the numbers 1 to 5 without a loop. You would write five print lines. Now imagine 1 to a million. Copying lines is clearly impossible.
A loop lets you describe the repeating work once and tell the computer how many times, or how long, to do it. The computer handles the repetition for you.
The while Loop
A while loop keeps running as long as a condition stays true. Use it when you do not know in advance how many times you will repeat.

codes.python:
i = 1
while i <= 5:
    print(i)
    i += 1     # always move closer to ending the loop

blocks.text: The loop checks the condition, runs the block if it is true, then checks again, over and over, until the condition becomes false.
The most common while loop mistake is forgetting to move toward the end. If the condition never becomes false, the loop runs forever.

codes.python:
i = 1
while i <= 5:
    print(i)
    # forgot i += 1, so this never ends

blocks.text: Always make sure something inside the loop changes the condition toward false. If your program freezes and prints endlessly, you likely have an infinite loop.
The for Loop
A for loop is ideal when you know how many times to repeat. It bundles the start, the condition, and the step into one tidy line.

codes.python:
for i in range(1, 6):   # i takes the values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
    print(i)

blocks.text: The for loop is the workhorse of counting. When you know the number of repetitions up front, it is cleaner than a while loop.

content.title: 3. Looping Over a Range of Numbers

blocks.text: Counting through a range is so common that it is worth understanding well. In Python, range produces a sequence of numbers for the loop to walk through.
Notice that range starts at 0 by default and stops just before the end number. This off by one behaviour is normal, but it surprises many beginners at first.
Looping Over a Collection
Very often you want to visit every item in a list. A for each style loop does this without you ever touching an index.
This reads almost like English: for each fruit in fruits, print the fruit. It is cleaner and safer than looping by index when you just need each item.
Sometimes you need both the item and its position. Most languages give you a clean way to get both at once.
Here i is the position and fruit is the value. This is handy when you need to know where in the list you are.
Stopping Early with break
Sometimes you want to leave a loop before it naturally finishes. The break keyword stops the loop immediately.
break is perfect for searching: once you find what you want, there is no reason to keep looping.
The continue keyword skips the rest of the current turn and jumps straight to the next one.
break leaves the loop entirely. continue only skips the current turn and keeps looping. Mixing them up is a common early confusion.
Nested Loops
You can put a loop inside another loop. For every single turn of the outer loop, the inner loop runs all the way through.

codes.python:
for i in range(1, 4):        # outer loop: rows
    for j in range(1, 4):    # inner loop: columns
        print(i, j)

blocks.text: Nested loops are the secret behind grids, tables, and pattern problems. Picture the outer loop as rows and the inner loop as columns.
One pattern shows up in countless problems: keep a running value and update it on every turn. This is called an accumulator.

codes.python:
numbers = [4, 8, 15, 16, 23]
total = 0
for n in numbers:
    total += n      # add each number to the running total
print(total)        # 66

blocks.text: Start with a beginning value, then update it inside the loop. The same idea powers summing, counting, and building up a result.
Searching With a Loop
A very common use of a loop is to search a list for something, then stop once you find it.

codes.python:
names = ["Amit", "Riya", "Sara"]
found = False
for name in names:
    if name == "Riya":
        found = True
        break
print(found)     # True

blocks.text: Loop through the items, check each one, and break as soon as you find a match. Using break here avoids wasting time after the answer is known.
Combining a loop with a comparison lets you find the biggest or smallest value in a list, a classic beginner exercise.
Start by assuming the first value is the best, then update whenever you find something larger. This pattern generalises to smallest, longest, and more.
Common Loop Patterns
These small patterns cover a huge amount of everyday looping.

items: Sum: add each item to a running total.
Count: add one to a counter when a condition holds.
Max or min: track the best value seen so far.
Build: start with an empty list or string and add to it each turn.
Search: check each item and break when found.

blocks.text: Loops do not only count up. You can count down just as easily, which is handy for reversing or working from the end.
The third value in range is the step. A step of minus one walks the numbers downward instead of upward.
Looping Over the Characters of Text
Text is a sequence of characters, so you can loop over it just like a list, visiting one character at a time.

codes.python:
for ch in "hello":
    print(ch)      # h, e, l, l, o on separate lines

blocks.text: This is the foundation of countless string problems, from counting letters to checking spelling.

content.title: 9. A Loop That Runs at Least Once

blocks.text: Sometimes you need a loop to run once before checking whether to continue, like asking the user for input until it is valid.

codes.python:
simulated_inputs = ["no", "maybe", "yes"]
index = 0

while True:
    answer = simulated_inputs[index]  # simulate reading input without blocking on stdin
    index += 1
    print(f"Type yes to continue: {answer}")
    if answer == "yes":
        break         # leave the loop when the condition is met

blocks.text: Here the loop always runs at least once, and break decides when to stop. This is a clean way to repeat until something valid happens.
A Worked Example: Average of Numbers
Let us combine the accumulator pattern with a count to compute an average.

codes.python:
numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40]
total = 0
for n in numbers:
    total += n
average = total / len(numbers)
print(average)     # 25.0

blocks.text: Add everything up in the loop, then divide by how many there were. Sum and count together give you the average.
Here is a classic beginner problem that ties loops, conditions, and strings together.
Loop over each character, check whether it is a vowel, and add to a counter when it is. Small pattern, huge number of uses.
Building a New List in a Loop
A very common task is to build up a new list, one item at a time, as you loop.

codes.python:
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4]
squares = []
for n in numbers:
    squares.append(n * n)
print(squares)     # [1, 4, 9, 16]

blocks.text: Start with an empty list, then add to it on each turn. This pattern transforms one list into another and appears everywhere.

content.title: 11. A Worked Example: FizzBuzz for a Range

blocks.text: Now let us run FizzBuzz across many numbers by wrapping the decision inside a loop. This is the classic combination of loops and conditionals.
The loop provides the numbers, and the conditions decide what to print for each. Together they solve a real problem in a few clean lines.
Loops and conditionals are a team. Most useful programs combine repeating work with decisions made on each turn.

items: Forgetting to update the variable in a while loop, causing an infinite loop
Off by one errors, looping one time too many or too few
Confusing break, which exits, with continue, which skips one turn
Changing a list while looping over it, which causes surprising bugs
Doing work inside a loop that only needs to happen once outside it

blocks.text: When a loop misbehaves, print the loop variable on every turn. Watching it change, or fail to change, usually reveals the bug immediately.
When should I use while versus for?
Use for when you know how many times to repeat. Use while when you repeat until some condition changes and you do not know the count in advance.
Why does my range stop one early?
range stops just before the end number by design. To include the end, add one to it.
What is the difference between break and continue?
break leaves the loop completely. continue skips only the current turn and keeps looping.
My loop never stops, what is wrong?
Almost always a while loop where the condition never becomes false. Make sure something inside changes it toward the end.

items: Loop: code that repeats.
Iteration: one single turn of a loop.
Counter: a variable that tracks the loop position.
break: stop the loop immediately.
continue: skip to the next turn.
Accumulator: a running value built up across turns.
Print the numbers 1 to 20 with a loop.
Sum the first N numbers.
Print a multiplication table for a given number.
Count how many even numbers are in a list.
Find the largest and smallest number in a list.

blocks.text: Loops let you repeat work. Next you will use them on real number and pattern problems, where loops truly shine.
